https://www.census.gov/data/developers.html

This was the link I used to request an API Key:
https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html


The main question I want to answer regarding the where is whether do crimes occur more closer or father from the highway. I am using the following libraries and an env file for my api to access census data. Finally I load the dallas crime data
```{r}

library(dotenv) # Import env file with my api key
library(tidycensus) # Import library for census data

library(tigris) # Gets outlines for counties
library(ggplot2) # Plotting map
library(dplyr) # For math for data analysis
library(sf) # Checks what touches dallas county
library(ggimage) # For interstate and highway shields

# Load the file from the parent directory
load_dot_env(file = "../.env")

# Pulls api key from the env file
census_api_key(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"), install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)

# loads table
master_analysis <- read.csv("../Dallas_Crimes_dallas_Website_For_Where.csv")

```


Here, I fetch the population data of how many people live in each zip code in dallas county. This will allow us to get an accurate proportion, and this way, the number of crimes won't get skewed towards the zip codes that have a higher population. this way we can get a more accurate answer of how safe each zip code really is.
```{r}
# --- 2. FETCH POPULATION DATA (Using the API) ---
# We switch to 'acs5' for 2020 to ensure ZCTA availability
pop_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "zcta",
  variables = "B01003_001", # ACS variable for Total Population
  year = 2020,
  survey = "acs5"
) %>%
  # Clean the names to match your crime data
  mutate(zip_clean = as.character(as.integer(gsub("ZCTA5 ", "", NAME)))) %>%
  select(zip_clean, population = estimate) # ACS uses 'estimate' instead of 'value'

```


Here, we are loading and preping the crime data. First I am getting the zip code as an integer, so this way we can get rid of any accidental decimal points. Next, I categorize whether the crime is a Violent Crime, Property Crime, or Society Crime. I do this by using key words in the "Call (911) Problem" column. Based on these key words, we can sort it into what crime actually occurs in which zip code. Finally, we filter the other columns out, because they may be non crime reporting 911 calls.
```{r}
# --- 3. LOAD & PREP CRIME DATA ---
# Replace your old crime_summary with this new "Categorized" version
crime_summary <- master_analysis %>%
  mutate(
    zip_clean = as.character(as.integer(Zip.Code)),
    
    # This maps the 911 call descriptions to the 3 NIBRS categories
    category = case_when(
      # PERSONS (Violent)
      grepl("ASSAULT|ROBBERY|SHOOTING|STABBING|MURDER|KIDNAP", Call..911..Problem, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Persons (Violent)",
      
      # PROPERTY
      grepl("THEFT|BURGLARY|VANDAL|PROPERT|FORGERY|FRAUD", Call..911..Problem, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Property",
      
      # SOCIETY (Drugs/Weapons/Order)
      grepl("DRUG|NARCOTIC|WEAPON|GUN|PROSTITUT|GAMBL", Call..911..Problem, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "Society",
      
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  # Filter for Dallas zips and remove the "Other" category to keep the map clean
  filter(grepl("^75", zip_clean), category != "Other") %>%
  group_by(zip_clean, category) %>%
  summarise(total_incidents = n(), .groups = "drop")
```


Here, we are organizing our zip codes so that we will only receive data for dallas county. We do this by getting the 2020 outlines for every zip code, and we filter by making sure every zip code starts with 75 to make sure it is a part of or at least close to dallas county. Next, we import all the texas highways, but then we use the filter function to be specific to dallas county. This is why some areas of highways are cut off, bceuase parts of them are not in dallas county. (EX PGBT)
```{r}
# --- 4. FETCH GEOMETRY (Maps & Roads) ---
dallas_zips <- tigris::zctas(year = 2020, cb = TRUE) %>%
  filter(grepl("^75", ZCTA5CE20))

tx_highways <- tigris::primary_secondary_roads(state = "TX", year = 2020)

# --- 4. FETCH GEOMETRY (Maps & Roads) ---
dallas_highways <- st_intersection(tx_highways, st_union(dallas_zips)) %>%
  filter(
    # 1. Keep all Interstates
    RTTYP == "I" | 
    # 2. Keep the specific Tollways
    grepl("Dall.*North.*Tollway|George.*Bush.*Tpk", FULLNAME, ignore.case = TRUE) |
    # 3. FIX: Only keep US-75, exclude US-175
    # The \\b75\\b ensures it doesn't match 175 or 750
    (RTTYP == "U" & grepl("\\b75\\b", FULLNAME))
  ) %>%
  mutate(road_type = case_when(
    RTTYP == "I" ~ "Interstate",
    grepl("\\b75\\b", FULLNAME) ~ "US Highway",
    TRUE ~ "Tollway"
  ))
```



This is where we reduce the boundries to make sure that we are only getting the data for dallas county. Although we already made sure that our zip code started in 75, we need to make sure that our zip codes are all in dallas county. The reason the step earlier of making sure all our zip codes started with 75, is that it can now take less time to cut down our zip codes to make sure that it is in dallas county. This will make the processing time a bit quicker. Finally, we have the highway sheilds so that I can label them on the maps.
```{r}
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
# --- 5. THE DALLAS COUNTY FILTER ---
# 1. Get the official Dallas County Boundary (FIPS 113 for Dallas, TX)
dallas_county_outline <- counties(state = "TX", cb = TRUE) %>%
  filter(NAME == "Dallas")

# 2. Filter Zip Codes to ONLY those that touch Dallas County
map_base <- dallas_zips %>%
  mutate(match_id = as.character(as.integer(ZCTA5CE20))) %>%
  # This is the "Cookie Cutter" step
  st_filter(dallas_county_outline, .predicate = st_intersects) %>%
  left_join(pop_data, by = c("match_id" = "zip_clean"))

# --- 5.5 STABLE HIGHWAY ICONS (Local Files) ---
highway_shields <- data.frame(
  name = c("I-635", "I-35E", "I-30", "US-75", "DNT", "PGBT", "I-45", "I-20"),
  long = c(-96.80, -96.87, -96.72, -96.73, -96.82, -96.75, -96.75, -96.78),
  lat  = c(32.925, 32.82, 32.795, 32.96, 32.85, 33.00, 32.69, 32.65),
  # Matching your screenshot names exactly
  image = c(
    "I-635.svg.png", 
    "I-35E_(TX).png",                            # If this fails, rename the file to .png manually
    "I-30.svg.png", 
    "US_75.svg.png", 
    "Toll_Texas_Dallas_North_Tollway.svg.png", 
    "Toll_Texas_President_George_Bush_Turnpike.svg.png", # Same here
    "I-45_(TX).svg.png",                             # And here
    "I-20.svg.png"
  )
)
```




Finally, here we are plotting our data. First, I have a global theme to kepp the grpahs looking the same. next, I have a mapping function that helps keep the three maps with the same zoom, highway layers, and crime calculations. After that, we graph our three maps and highlight the zip codes accordingly. However, we have a problem, because for our property crime map, there are some areas that show an extremely high crime denisty. This is because there are more crimes that occur than residents that actually live in that zip code. This could be because there are many more shopping centers compared to residential areas for example. This is really good in terms of which areas are safer, because it tells you what areas you are more likely to experience a crime, but it is likely exagerated when you are in a residential area in that zip code. This is known as the denominator effect. 
```{r}
# --- 6. INDIVIDUAL PLOTS WITH NA LABELS ---
options(scipen = 999)

# Global Theme for consistency
map_theme <- theme_void() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
  )

# Function to generate the map to keep logic identical for all three
generate_crime_map <- function(cat_name, fill_high, title_text) {
  
  # Filter crime data for just this specific category
  category_data <- crime_summary %>% filter(category == cat_name)
  
  # Join with the map base so "Empty" Zips stay in the table
  plot_data <- map_base %>%
    left_join(category_data, by = c("match_id" = "zip_clean")) %>%
    mutate(crime_rate = (total_incidents / population) * 1000)

  ggplot() +
    # 1. The Map Polygons (Black outlines, White for NA areas)
    geom_sf(data = plot_data, aes(fill = crime_rate), color = "black", size = 0.1) +
    
    # 2. The NA Text (Only in zips with zero reported incidents)
    geom_sf_text(data = filter(plot_data, is.na(total_incidents)), 
                 aes(label = "NA"), size = 1.8, color = "grey60") +
    
    # 3. Highways & Shields (Standardized for all maps)
    geom_sf(data = dallas_highways, aes(size = road_type), color = "#ff9800", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_point(data = highway_shields, aes(x = long, y = lat), 
               color = "white", size = 7, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
    geom_image(data = highway_shields, aes(x = long, y = lat, image = image), size = 0.045) +
    
    # 4. Color Scale with Log Transformation
    scale_fill_gradient(
        low = "#f0f9ff", 
        high = fill_high, 
        na.value = "white",
        name = "Rate per 1k", 
        
        # This is the "Log" part the professor asked for
        trans = "log10", 
        
        # This keeps the scale "the same" (readable numbers instead of scientific notation)
        breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000),
        labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1000")
    ) +
    
    scale_size_manual(values = c("Interstate" = 0.7, "Tollway" = 0.4, "US Highway" = 0.4), guide = "none") +
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-97.02, -96.58), ylim = c(32.62, 33.02), expand = FALSE) +
    map_theme + labs(title = title_text)
}

# GENERATE THE THREE PLOTS
# We use different colors: Red for Violent, Blue for Property, Green for Society
p1 <- generate_crime_map("Persons (Violent)", "#b71c1c", "Dallas: Violent Crime Density")
p2 <- generate_crime_map("Property", "#01579b", "Dallas: Property Crime Density")
p3 <- generate_crime_map("Society", "#1b5e20", "Dallas: Society Crime Density")

# Display them (In a PDF Knit, these will appear one after another)
p1
p2
p3
```


** Data Analysis **
This is the part where I will be analyzing whether dallas crimes occur closer or father from the highway


However, based on these graphs, one major problem that we can see is that at least one of the highways I listed touches almost every single zip code in Dallas County. Therefore doing a standard t-test where we have the compare zip codes that have a highway vs not having a highway won't help us here, because the data will be extremely skewed. 

Instead, we can compare it to 2 or more highways in a zip code vs 1 or less highways in a zip code, because that will be more balanced and it will help decrease our bias. Since we plotted our heat maps relative to violent crime, property crime, and society crime, we will be conducting 3 seperate t-tests for each type of crime


Setting up Data for our tests:
```{r}
# 1. Count unique highway intersections per Zip Code
intersections_list <- st_intersects(map_base, dallas_highways)
map_base$highway_count <- lengths(intersections_list)

# 2. Create the Intensity Group (2+ vs 1 or less)
map_base <- map_base %>%
  mutate(intensity_group = ifelse(highway_count >= 2, "High_Intensity", "Low_Intensity"))

# 3. Drop geometry for faster statistical processing
base_stats_df <- map_base %>% st_drop_geometry()
```

1. Violent Crime:
```{r}
# Prepare Violent Crime Data
violent_df <- base_stats_df %>%
  left_join(filter(crime_summary, category == "Persons (Violent)"), by = c("match_id" = "zip_clean")) %>%
  mutate(crime_rate = (total_incidents / population) * 1000) %>%
  filter(!is.na(crime_rate))

# Run T-Test
t_violent <- t.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = violent_df)
print(t_violent)

# Run Wilcox Test, because t-test did not give p-value we wanted since our n-value which is the number of zip codes, is not too high at n = 65, which potentially skewed our results
w_violent <- wilcox.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = violent_df)
print(w_violent)
```

2. Property Crime:
```{r}
# Prepare Property Crime Data
property_df <- base_stats_df %>%
  left_join(filter(crime_summary, category == "Property"), by = c("match_id" = "zip_clean")) %>%
  mutate(crime_rate = (total_incidents / population) * 1000) %>%
  filter(!is.na(crime_rate))

# Run T-Test
t_property <- t.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = property_df)
print(t_property)

# Run Wilcox Test, because t-test did not give p-value we wanted since our n-value which is the number of zip codes, is not too high at n = 65, which potentially skewed our results
w_property <- wilcox.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = property_df)
print(w_property)
```

3. Society Crime:
```{r}
# Prepare Society Crime Data
society_df <- base_stats_df %>%
  left_join(filter(crime_summary, category == "Society"), by = c("match_id" = "zip_clean")) %>%
  mutate(crime_rate = (total_incidents / population) * 1000) %>%
  filter(!is.na(crime_rate))

# Run T-Test
t_society <- t.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = society_df)
print(t_society)

# Run Wilcox Test, because t-test did not give p-value we wanted since our n-value which is the number of zip codes, is not too high at n = 65, which potentially skewed our results
w_society <- wilcox.test(crime_rate ~ intensity_group, data = society_df)
print(w_society)
```
Okay so I tried the t-test and that was not giving me the p-value that I wanted, so I assumed the outliers were the problem. Then I also tried the Wilcoxon-test because that eliminates the problem of outliers, but even though for violent crime it was treding in the right direction, none of the values from either test were below 5%. Then I realized it is because my n-value, which is 65 zip codes, is too small so even though my theory may be true that you are safer farther away from a highway, I am not able to prove this because we are not getting the required data. Based on our observations, there is not a major difference in safety in regards to being closer or farther away from a highway from a statistical sense. However, from a practical standpoint, the crime rate doubled, but because our p values were never less than 5% we can't back it up.

This is most likely a type II error (An error where there is most likely an effect in the real world but my test is not catching it).
